5. Discussion
5.1 Critical evaluation of the design
The results show a working connection between photographed handwriting, stored writer profiles
and physical pen movement. The most useful outcome is that several styles remain both readable
and identifiable after being reconstructed from stored glyphs. Performance depends on the
writing style and the requested operation. The discussion below relates those differences to the
decisions made in Design.
5.1.1 Interpretation of results
Reproduction preserves useful writer characteristics.The reader recovers 84.41% of the
physical characters according to the edit-based score. Seven of the eleven writers exceed 85%,
with the strongest four above 93%. This is close to the pooled character target, but the spread
between writers matters more than the 0.59 percentage-point shortfall alone. A user selecting a
separated style receives a more consistent result than one selecting a strongly connected style.
The design therefore demonstrates the intended function, while its operating range is clearer than
a single average would suggest.
Writer identification remains correct on 86.41% of the reproduced lines and all fourteen page
pools. The normalised geometric result adds a different check. It compares actual stroke positions
with original handwriting, while accounting for the fact that a writer does not produce the same
word identically each time. The ordinary-reference result retains 86.68% of measured natural
agreement when writers are weighted equally. Choosing the nearest reference gives 87.89%.
Agreement between these two approaches is useful because the favourable relative result does
not depend entirely on selecting one best-looking original.
These percentages need their measurement definitions. They are relative geometric scores on
83 repeated words, not percentages of correctly written characters. The subset also contains
shorter, more common words than the complete passage set. It supports a measured comparison
with natural variation, without establishing that every sentence or writer meets the proposal’s
stylistic target. Direct shape measures and recognition outcomes are complementary, since
recognition-based evaluation depends on the evaluating model [42, p. 2].
The individual writers show why both checks are needed. Writer 150 has strong geometric
agreement relative to the natural baseline, but its line identification is lower. Writer T is identified
correctly on every physical line while its character recovery and geometric agreement are weaker.
The classifier can therefore retain enough distinctive cues to recognise a writer even when
individual forms or joins differ. It also helps select synthesis candidates, so a second evaluation
using that classifier is partly tied to the selection criterion. The geometric test provides a separate
view of the resulting strokes.
The gap between isolated shapes and complete words is a design result.The earlier character
examples show that many stored letterforms can be reproduced closely. Whole-word comparison
retains the spacing and joins between those forms. Small errors in advance width accumulate
61

[PDF PAGE 80]
D.R. Braune Discussion
along a word, and a connector can change the shape around two otherwise reasonable glyphs.
This explains why a convincing isolated character does not guarantee an equally close complete
word.
Word-height normalisation improves the whole-word comparison relative to line-height normal-
isation. Some disagreement therefore comes from the chosen size reference as well as the ink
path. It would be misleading to interpret the larger score as an improvement to the machine, be-
cause the physical page is unchanged. The useful conclusion is that the assessment should show
its normalisation and include the raw examples. The remaining differences in those examples
still need engineering attention, particularly for cursive styles.
Original-handwriting classification is close to the intended accuracy.The reader’s 94.06%
pooled character accuracy is 0.94 percentage points below the proposal’s target. Its public
and photographed subsets give similar aggregate scores, which supports using one line-based
architecture for both inputs. However, the personal writers do not all give the same result. An
overall average should therefore accompany the separate populations rather than replace them.
Writer identification reaches 98.08% on the 156 original validation lines, with all eleven writer
groups correct after pooling. Stroke normalisation is important here because the physical pen
cannot reproduce each contributor’s original pen thickness. The classifier instead receives a
more consistent stroke width. This reduces one avoidable difference between original and robot
writing, but it does not remove differences in camera conditions, letter construction or the amount
of evidence in a short line.
The reader follows the CNN, BiLSTM and CTC approach discussed in the literature [12, pp. 4–5].
Its result supports that choice for this dataset. Different train/test partitions and decoding rules
prevent a direct ranking against published accuracy figures. The current test also does not separate
errors caused by the network from those caused by a poor line crop. A future comparison should
retain a fixed set of manually checked crops to measure those contributions separately.
Reproduction speed is achieved in the tested requests.All 25 completed ODROID jobs meet
the four-second-per-character limit. These are complete request timings, including generation
and drawing, so they are more useful than a calculation from commanded feed alone. The slowest
43-character request leaves only 5.39 seconds of total margin. The short jobs therefore have less
room for additional processing or pen movements.
The nine 378-character requests vary from 507.57 to 1085.01 seconds. Equal text length does
not imply an equal motion job. Different writer profiles produce different path lengths, numbers
of pen changes and synthesis work. This variation is consistent with a system that reproduces
writer geometry rather than drawing every character using one fixed font. The recorded success
applies to the tested requests, starting at 43 characters. Very short requests would need their own
timing evidence because fixed preparation costs are less diluted.
Classification time is the main embedded performance limitation.The two measured
requests exceed their allowances by 31.76 and 28.94 seconds. Networks account for 67.6% of the
combined time, making numerical inference the first optimisation target. The stage records also
show why network acceleration alone is insufficient. For the 500-character request, image stages
already take 16.14 seconds against a 14.50-second total allowance. Even removing network time
entirely would leave that request over its limit. For 982 characters, the image stages leave 9.74
seconds for networks that currently take 38.67 seconds.
62

[PDF PAGE 81]
D.R. Braune Discussion
The supporting benchmark reduces network time by a factor of 2.76 while retaining the recorded
reader text. It changes both batching and backend, so it identifies an implementation opportunity
rather than a measured embedded improvement from batching alone. The resolution experiment
is less suitable. Reducing image size changes the detected lines and decoded output, so its speed
gain is not an equivalent replacement. A useful optimisation must preserve the crop ordering and
predictions as well as reduce runtime.
Repeated dimensions support the mechanical arrangement.The ten new square-and-
triangle samples provide a better check than one specimen. All 70 feature lengths are within
0.5 mm, with a mean absolute error of 0.297 mm and a largest error of 0.49 mm. These results
support the calibrated belt transmission and the use of one motor to drive the two sides of
the moving gantry through a shared shaft. The arrangement avoids having two independently
commanded motors set the rail position, while bearing alignment and frame stiffness still affect
motion.
The signs and grouping of the errors are useful. Square lengths shift above and below nominal
between samples, while the two triangle slopes often move in opposite directions. A fixed
steps-per-millimetre correction alone would not explain every change of sign. Rail alignment,
belt tension, pen restraint and the measurement contact convention are therefore reasonable items
to check before changing scale constants. The readings do not isolate one of these causes, so
they should not be used to claim a measured rail angle.
The smallest margin to the dimensional limit is 0.01 mm. With the caliper least count and
nib-edge convention unrecorded, there is little basis for adding an uncertainty guard band. The
result is that all supplied dimensions pass the stated numerical comparison. It is not a guarantee
of absolute pen position everywhere on the bed. A translated square can keep the same side
lengths. Repeated coordinates and overlaid drawings would extend this check to placement and
return accuracy.
5.1.2 Critical evaluation
Line recognition was the appropriate alternative to early character cuts.The proposal
allowed separated characters or connected groups. Reading complete lines avoids requiring
every letter boundary to be correct before recognising the text. CTC supports this by combining
possible alignments during training [14, pp. 2–3]. Known-transcript alignment is then used for
profile extraction. This separates the reading problem from the more demanding problem of
obtaining reusable character shapes.
The trade-off is that the network processes a long sequence and remains dependent on correct
line ownership. Touching lines or a clipped ascender can affect the complete sequence. The
intermediate masks, seams and crop figures in Design are therefore important practical tools.
They make it possible to identify which stage lost a stroke, rather than treating every incorrect
word as a network failure.
The glyph library suits the available offline samples.The inputs are page images, without
recorded pen positions over time. An example-based approach can use those images directly
and retain inspected letter shapes from a small collection of pages, as demonstrated by Haines et
al. [23, p. 4]. A sequence generator such as Graves’s instead uses ordered pen coordinates [3,
p. 18]. Learning that missing chronology would add another problem to the project.
63

[PDF PAGE 82]
D.R. Braune Discussion
Stored paths also make size, slant and machine coordinates controllable. Their finite context is
the main limitation. A writer changes a letter depending on its neighbours and often makes the
connection as part of that letter. Joining two separately stored shapes cannot reproduce every
such change. Increasing the number of random trials may find a better existing combination, but
cannot create a missing contextual form. Multi-character units and position-dependent variants
are therefore more directly connected to the observed cursive errors than simply increasing
candidate count.
The current system is still useful because it reaches eleven styles with explicit, inspectable
geometry. A larger learned generator could offer more contextual variation, but would require a
different preparation and training effort. A single reference at generation time does not remove
the need for that wider training corpus [22, p. 9]. The choice made here is appropriate to the
available samples and hardware, with its limits visible in the connected writers.
First-principles operation makes the implementation inspectable.The numerical imple-
mentation exposes forward passes, derivatives, CTC and parameter updates. The operation
checks in Design test these calculations using matched inputs, while the training records show
that the implementation can learn the required tasks. Close validation scores between imple-
mentations are useful supporting evidence, but do not by themselves establish that every training
operation is equivalent.
Training and inference place different demands on memory and execution time. The supplied
records show approximately 19 to 23 minutes per writer epoch and 111 to 122 minutes per reader
epoch. Float32 limits memory and computation cost, but the retained experiments do not isolate
precision as the cause of accuracy differences. Keeping the numerical definitions while batching
repeated work or compiling hot loops is a reasonable next step. Its effect should be checked with
the same inputs and saved outputs before using it in a timed ODROID qualification.
Mechanical simplicity has clear benefits and limits.Orthogonal axes give a direct relationship
between a Cartesian target and motor displacement. The shared drive shaft keeps the two sides
of the moving rail mechanically linked. These choices make fabrication, calibration and fault
finding manageable within the prototype budget. The repeated feature measurements support the
resulting dimensional performance.
Open-loop stepping still assumes that commanded pulses become real motion. A missed step is
not visible in the position counter. Calibration establishes the origin and travel scale, but cannot
detect a later loss of position. Controlled acceleration and a shared pulse schedule would address
starting load and direction-dependent timing. A stiffer holder and more consistent paper restraint
would reduce motion that is not represented in the step counts. These changes should be judged
using repeated physical drawings, since finer nominal microsteps alone do not establish better
pen accuracy [30].
The pen mechanism uses a geared motor, cam and a switch rather than a continuously positioned
third axis. It provides the two states needed for drawing and travel with simple control. The
springs accommodate page contact, but there is no measured pen-force loop. Changes in paper
support or pen friction can therefore alter the physical stroke even when the same trajectory is
commanded.
Economic feasibility.The author’s current prototype estimate is approximately R4 000. The
borrowed ODROID has no purchase cost for this build and will be returned. A repeat build would
64

[PDF PAGE 83]
D.R. Braune Discussion
need to include its replacement value. Reusable motors, rails and drivers keep the prototype
practical, while replaceable printed parts allow local changes without rebuilding the frame.
Preparation and training time also matter. Improving an existing numerical implementation
may be a more proportionate first step than replacing the complete computer or adopting a new
generator.
5.1.3 Unsolved problems
The first priority is classification speed with unchanged output. The measured stage times give a
clear order of work, beginning with network execution and then the image stages that already
exceed the short-request budget. Each optimisation should retain a fixed page set, crop count and
reference outputs, followed by a complete ODROID timing run.
The next reproduction priority is connected context. A controlled comparison should use the
same text, profiles, reader and physical setup, changing only the use of multi-character units or
contextual variants. This would test whether the proposed change improves the weaker writers
rather than only producing a more favourable example.
Mechanical qualification should add repeated bed coordinates and word overlays. The ten
supplied samples establish feature-length behaviour, but do not yet map placement across the
writing area. Those tests would also help separate frame geometry from pen-holder and page-
restraint effects.
5.1.4 Strong points of the design
The complete chain produces physical output in eleven stored styles, with every recorded page
pool identified correctly. The repeated dimensions remain within 0.5 mm and every completion-
confirmed drawing request meets its timing allowance. These are integrated outcomes rather
than isolated software demonstrations.
The system is also inspectable. A source crop can be followed through alignment, glyph paths,
layout and G-code to the machine. Numerical checks support the implemented calculations,
while the new geometric baseline checks physical shape without relying solely on a classifier.
Keeping these different forms of evidence separate makes the evaluation more useful when one
style or stage needs improvement.
5.1.5 Expected failure conditions
Strong cursive connections and missing contextual variants are the main reproduction limits.
Text outside the stored alphabet can also lack a suitable form. A preview is important when
a requested layout approaches the bed limits, since clamping an out-of-range path changes its
geometry.
Touching lines, page curvature and strong perspective can defeat preparation. A single global
deskew angle cannot remove local warping. Sparse writing also gives less evidence for estimating
orientation and writer identity. The writer classifier chooses among known classes, so an
unfamiliar writer can still receive a confident known label.
65

[PDF PAGE 84]
D.R. Braune Discussion
On the machine, changing belt tension, slipping couplers, increased carriage resistance or a
disturbed sheet can break the relationship between commanded and actual movement. End stops
and software abort handling assist recovery, but do not replace independent power isolation. The
stated dimensional and timing performance applies to the tested setup and requests, rather than
every load or environmental condition.
5.2 Considerations in the design
5.2.1 Ergonomics
The browser groups capture, text entry, writer selection and preview. Keeping generation separate
from physical execution lets the operator inspect a job before the gantry moves. The paper clamps
and camera support reduce repeated manual positioning. The operator must still fit the pen,
secure the sheet, calibrate the axes and check clearance. Clear feedback on calibration, job
completion and interruption is therefore as important as an attractive display.
5.2.2 Health and safety
The moving carriage, belts and pulleys create pinch points. The working area should remain clear
during drawing, with a reachable means of removing motor power. Limit switches and abort
checks reduce the chance of continued travel after a fault, but software can become unresponsive
and is not an independent isolator. Wiring restraint and access to the motor-driver area also
matter because the drivers dissipate heat.
The logic and motor circuits use separate low-voltage rails supplied by purchased adapters. The
pen transistor separates motor current from the GPIO signal. The installed circuit still lacks an
inductive-current recirculation diode, so adding the reverse-biased diode described in Design
is an appropriate protection improvement [43]. It should be fitted and checked before repeated
unattended operation.
5.2.3 Environmental impact
The borrowed computer will be returned and the main motion components can be reused. The
printed supports can be replaced individually, which reduces the need to discard an entire frame
after a design change. Digital previews reduce unnecessary trial drawings, although physical
paper and pen tests remain necessary for qualification. Motor holding current and long training
runs consume energy even when the visible output is small. The project has not metered those
contributions, so no numerical environmental-saving claim is made.
5.2.4 Social and legal impact
Reproducing a chosen writing style could help with personalised correspondence or with tasks
that are difficult for a person to write manually. These possible uses have not been evaluated
66

[PDF PAGE 85]
D.R. Braune Discussion
with users. The same capability can imitate another person’s writing, so authorised use and clear
identification of machine-produced material are important. The system should not be presented
as a means of validating signatures or authorship.
The five personal contributors supplied signed consent. Their samples and derived profiles should
remain under controlled access, with a stated purpose and retention period. These concerns follow
the personal-information considerations addressed in the Protection of Personal Information
Act [44, pp. 8–9, 11]. IAM material must also remain subject to its dataset terms. The prototype’s
local network arrangement limits the intended access scope, but is not evidence of a security
qualification.
5.2.5 Ethics clearance
Signed participant consent is held for the five personal contributors. An institutional clearance
or exemption reference is not established by the supplied records. Participant consent and
institutional approval are therefore treated as separate matters.
67

[PDF PAGE 86]
D.R. Braune Conclusion
6. Conclusion
6.1 Summary of the work completed
A handwriting robot was designed and built to recognise photographed text, identify a known
writer and reproduce new digital text in that writer’s style. The system combines page condition-
ing, line segmentation, neural recognition, stored glyph trajectories and a calibrated Cartesian
gantry. Eleven writer profiles are stored and exercised in physical reproduction.
6.2 Summary of observations and findings
The selected reader achieves 94.06% character accuracy and writer identification reaches 98.08%
on the recorded validation set. Physical reproduction gives 84.41% read-back character accuracy,
with seven writers above 85%. Writer identity is retained on 86.41% of reproduced lines and all
fourteen page pools. The measured shape correlation is 0.697, showing that recognisable identity
does not imply complete geometric similarity.
All 25 completion-confirmed ODROID reproduction jobs satisfy 4 s per character. The two
measured classification requests exceed their time allowances. Every measured square and
triangle length is within 0.5 mm of nominal, with a maximum difference of 0.37 mm. These
results establish dimensional performance on the specimens, while absolute placement and
repeatability need further qualification.
6.3 Contribution
The project demonstrates a complete path from offline handwriting samples to physical multi-
writer output. Its first-principles network implementation is supported by numerical checks
and trained models with scores close to the reference route. Explicit glyphs and G-code make
the relationship between image features and pen movement visible, allowing each stage to be
inspected and improved.
6.4 Suggestions for future work
The first priority is faster embedded classification without changing the detected lines or decoded
text. Batching and compiled numerical kernels should be measured on the ODROID. Context-
specific glyphs and multi-character units should then be tested on the more connected writers.
Repeated bed-coordinate measurements, word overlays and matched original-to-reproduced
sentences would strengthen the mechanical and stylistic evaluation. Improvements to motor
protection and pulse scheduling would complete the next hardware revision.

For that image, Otsu’s criterion selects bin 171. Its class masses are 0.07069375 and 0.92930625,

564.97942. The corresponding ratio threshold is(171+0.5)(1.2/256)=0.80390625.
In the Owen01 trace, the scores at+0.5○,+1.0○and+1.5○are 442973, 464105 and 439403. The
largest score across all seventeen angles is 464105, so the selected rotation is+1.0○.
In the recorded boundary between centres 38 and 61, ym=49.5 and hg=11.5 . At row 49 the
closed mask is zero, giving C=0.012[(49−49.5)/11.5]2=0.0000226843 . At column 283, the
selected predecessor is row 50 with stored cost 0.00641966. Its one-row change adds 0.02, so
the accumulated cost is 0.00641966+0.02+0.0000226843≃0.02644234.
At the implemented 0.012/0.02 setting, mean midpoint offset is 0.363 working pixels; removing
midpoint attraction raises it to 4.055 pixels.

A.1.3 Glyph extraction and reproduction calculations
For the V in that Owen line, frame 11 corresponds to state 11 of the blank-interleaved transcript.
Its log emission is −0.01988991and the three admissible predecessor scores are −13.91888,
−10.01139and−1.3624485. Equation 25 selects their maximum and gives V=−0.01988991−
1.3624485=−1.3823384. Backtracking assignsVthe frame interval[11,12).
The refined right boundary of this V is source column 193. Although smoothing gives p193=2.8
and the positive-column reference is 14.36, the raw ink count at column 193 is zero. The explicit
blank-column rule therefore overrides 2.8/14.36 and assigns zero cut cost.
A traced point on this V is (x,y)=(173,59) , with left cut xL =146 , baseline b=107 ,
hx =38 and tanφ=−0.0787017 . Equation 27 gives v=48/38=1.263158 and u0 =27/38−
1.263158(−0.0787017)=0.809939. After the implementation’s three-decimal intermediate
rounding and measured post-trim shift δ=0.4472489 , the stored point is (u,v)=(0.363,1.263)
and the recorded lead is 0.447 x-heights.
For unit-length descriptor vg and the normalised median reference rc for character c, the prior
distance is d(g,c)=1−v Tg rc. Internal consensus instead uses pairwise L1 descriptor distances
and chooses the medoid with the lowest total distance. Dylan’s first storeda variant has recorded
prior distance 0.114. Recomputing the pairwise rule on all nine final stored variants gives the
smallest total distance, 33.3413, for variant index 4; the other totals range from 34.4306 to
42.9091.
In the generated Owen sentence “Writing with style.”, the first placement call, after calibration
and jitter, uses (u,v)=(−0.01134565,1.47270173) , lead l=0.25117988 , zero shear and drift,
and hmmx =4 . With the initial placement origin (0,0) , Equation 29 gives x=4(0.25117988−
0.01134565)=0.9593369 mm andy=4(1.47270173)=5.8908069 mm.
The final Owen profile’s stored glyph distances have median ̃d=0.18355 . Equation 30 gives
λ=clip[(0.18355−0.24)/0.08,0,1]=0.
For the recorded Owen candidate 1, the 19-character target “Writing with style.” differs from its
reader output by one substitution, giving A=18/19=0.9473684 . The selected-writer posterior is
P=0.5786133, so Equation 31 givesJ=0.7184359.
In the worked Owen example, three pre-repair trials use the fixed text “Writing with style.”,
seeds 2026, 3003 and 3980, and the selected eleven-writer shape model with an explicit width
fraction of 0.17. Candidate 1 has(A,P,J)=(0.947,0.579,0.718) , while candidate 3 has the same
character score but (P,J)=(0.464,0.623) . The combined criterion therefore selects candidate 1.
The generated Owen trajectory has x0 =0.9593369 mm and y1 =6.6340616 mm. A
point (2.9829210,5.3303251) mm is placed using the configured origin (0,251.3) mm,
margins (15,10) mm, unit fit scale and zero line shift. Equation 32 gives (xm,y m)=
(17.0235840,239.9962635) mm. Three-decimal file emission writes this point as X17.024
Y239.996, connecting the trajectory calculation to the motion segment examined in Sec-
tion 3.3.6.

For this same generated file, the unrounded distance accumulators are Dd =139.0263729 mm
and Du=158.1555743 mm. At Fd =900 and Fu=2400 mm/min, with 56 pen transitions and
two 0.35 s dwell settings, Equation 33 givestnom=9.2684249+3.9538894+19.6=32.8223142 s.
The job metadata reports 32.8 s after rounding.
The Owen job contains 58 pen transitions: its recorded components are 9.249 s drawing, 3.198 s
travel and 58(0.35)=20.3 s dwell, giving 32.747 s in total. Thus dwell contributes about 62% of
this nominal budget; across the four jobs it contributes approximately 61–65%. These estimates
exclude the execution costs stated above and are not additional R3 timing measurements.

Applying this vote to the first two archived Owen01 crops gives ink weights 20204 and 21750,
with Owen probabilities 0.9996674 and 0.9999279 from the selected 0.17-width model. The recor-
ded page-weight calculation gives pOwen=(20204×0.9996674+21750×0.9999279)/41954≃
0.9998024. This is a two-crop calculation trace, not the full-page evaluation reported in Results.
